In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery of a novel metabolic pathway that is up-regulated in cancer cell lines, which may represent a new target to be exploited for the development of novel anticancer therapies.
a new transcriptional event associated with cancer cell lines, which may lead to a new strategy for cancer treatment.
the characterization of two large-scale transcription events that are common to cancer cell lines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

cancer cells are not only characterized by the overexpression of oncogenes and the down-regulation of tumor suppressor genes, but also by the failure to overexpression a large set of genes coding for membrane and extracellular receptors and transporters, which is putatively caused, at least in part, by the lack of activity of AP-1.

the failure in up-regulating a diverse set of membrane and extracellular genes is associated with an increased activity of BCAT2, which leads to a higher production of succinyl-CoA, an important intermediate of the TCA cycle.

the epithelial mesenchymal transition is an event that is associated to a metabolic change that involves a large scale down-regulation of genes involved in the degradation and transport of branched chain-amino acids.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cancer cells have a different transcriptional program from healthy dividing cells, which is associated with the upregulation of genes coding for enzymes involved in branched chain amino-acids catabolism, and this upregulation can be exploited for therapeutic purposes.
cancer cell lines have a unique transcriptional signature that can be used for their classification.

cancer cells have an altered transcriptional profile that leads them to fail in expressing a set of genes coding for membrane and extracellular components, which is putatively caused for an altered activity of the AP1 complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cancer cell lines can be used to identify novel therapeutic targets.
cancer cells are characterized by the up-regulation (or down-regulation) of specific transcriptional pathways that can be exploited to design new therapies.
cancer cell lines are transcriptionally characterized by a large-scale upregulation pattern associated to the epithelial-mensenchymal transition.
